rules.name: A. Where the address rules run (ordering)
rules.where: Phonemizer.phonemize: a pass after TextNormalizer.linkLabels and before custom.mark (TextNormalizer.addresses(_:british:)), or the readStreets pattern inside normalize, extended so it can replace a whole mark
rules.trigger: Hosts rules B to O. It runs once on the raw text and rewrites only address pieces.
rules.reads_as: Plain words, or digit groups that later stages read as they are. 'Beverly Hills, CA 90210' becomes 'Beverly Hills, California nine oh two one oh', and later stages see only ordinary words.
rules.risks: Since the first draft, the fix3/reading merge added TextNormalizer.readStreets. It reads 'St.' with custom-lexicon marks in view, so '7 Elm St. now' passes and the draft's claim that it reads 'Elm sˈAntˌi' is out of date. That pattern sees marked words around a match but skips any match inside a mark. Many address pieces are themselves marked terms: CA, GA, IL, IA, AR, PR, MP, PE, SE, PO and MD (case-insensitive, so 'Md.' too), the USPS 'DR', and the words Room, Box and Square. Marked place and street names include Elm, Willow, Front, Fleet, Spring, Ventura, Redwood, Sycamore, Phoenix, Jasper, Oxford, Georgia, Island, Bellevue, Cupertino, Redmond, Menlo, Mesa and Ada. So either run before custom.mark (simpler), or let the in-normalize pass replace whole marks. The pass must call ShoutedSentences itself, because unshout runs after marking. Emit number words without hyphens, because the British voice reads 'ninety-nine' differently from 'ninety nine'. Run before the range, units and clock/ratio rules. App path: the speech-test harness phonemizes whole lines, but the app splits sentences first. Tokenizer.titleContinues only rejoins after Dr., Mr., Mrs., Ms., Mt., St. and the titles, so 'Rd.', 'Ave.', 'Ste.', 'Apt.', 'Fl.', 'Rm.', 'Ore.' or 'N.Y.' before a capital may be split off before any rule sees it ('Elm Rd.' + 'Suite 3'). Add them to runOnTitles, or test the app path separately.

rules.name: B. Address number reading (helper)
rules.where: TextNormalizer helper built on NumberWords; used by rules C, D (Hwy), G and H
rules.trigger: A number in an address slot only: a house number (rule C); a Suite/Ste/Apt/Unit/Room/Rm/Floor/Fl/Bldg/Building number (rule G); a P.O. Box number; or a 3-digit route number (rule H).
rules.reads_as: 1–2 digits: the cardinal (42 → forty-two). 3 digits abc: a00 → 'a hundred' (300 three hundred); a0c → 'a oh c' (903 nine oh three, 101 one oh one); otherwise a, then the cardinal of bc (123 one twenty-three, 214 two fourteen, 350 three fifty). 4 digits: a000 → 'a thousand' (2000, 9000); ab00 → 'ab hundred' (1600 sixteen hundred, 4400 forty-four hundred, 1500 fifteen hundred); ab0d → 'ab oh d' (1005 ten oh five, 2005 twenty oh five); otherwise ab then cd (2041 twenty forty-one, 1010 ten ten, 4545 forty-five forty-five). 5 or more digits: one digit at a time, with 0 read 'oh', except round thousands. A trailing capital is its letter name (221B, 4B, 4C). Emit the letter A so it reads ˈA, not the article.
rules.risks: These are the US patterns. 3-digit numbers are also read digit by digit ('nine two three'); the ESL Cafe street-number guide lists both, and reads 5+ digits one at a time with 'oh'. This set uses the grouped form. British readers often say 3-digit house and room numbers digit by digit, so 221B and Rm. 214 are US-only cases (open question). Apply this reading only in the slots above: a bare number keeps its cardinal ('We drove 350 miles', 'I bought 1005 shares' are frozen). misaki's year-style reading already matches every 4-digit pattern except ab0d (1005 is 'one thousand five' today), which is exactly why a year must never reach this helper ('In 2005 Ocean Drive was repaved' is frozen; see rule C).

rules.name: C. Numbered street address
rules.trigger: A number (\d{1,5}, an optional capital, optionally '-' and a second number). Then an optional direction (N|S|E|W|NE|NW|SE|SW|North|South|East|West, optional period); it must be followed by a name, not directly by the type. Then 1–4 name tokens. A token is one of: a capitalised word with a lower-case letter (or all capitals inside an all-capitals address); a single capital; an ordinal \d{1,3}(st|nd|rd|th|ST|ND|RD|TH). Any token may follow St./Mt./Ft. Then a street type with an optional period: Street|St|Avenue|Ave|Av|Road|Rd|Drive|Dr|Boulevard|Blvd|Lane|Ln|Way|Court|Ct|Place|Pl|Parkway|Pkwy|Highway|Hwy|Terrace|Terr|Ter|Crescent|Cres|Square|Sq|Circle|Cir|Trail|Trl|Plaza|Plz|Close|Grove|Gardens|Gdns|Mews|Alley|Pike|Turnpike|Tpke|Expressway|Expy|Freeway|Fwy. Or the number comes straight before 'Broadway'. Then an optional trailing direction and a boundary: end, whitespace, [,;:)!?] or a period. USPS capitals match with the capital abbreviations ('123 MAIN ST APT 4B', '450 OAK DR', where DR is a marked term, '4545 S 1ST ST'). Gates: (1) an abbreviated type (St, Ave, Rd, Dr, Blvd, …) fires subject only to the guards under risks. (2) A type spelled out in full (Street, Court, Square, Place, Way, Terrace, …) fires only after an address cue: at, on, to, from, near, off, opposite, 'address', 'is at', 'Ship to', 'Shipping address:', 'Deliver to', 'Return to:', or the start of a line. It never fires when a lower-case noun follows the type, or in a title-case headline.
rules.reads_as: The number from rule B, plus 'to' and the second number for a range. Then the direction word, the name, the full street type and the trailing direction. '123 W 42nd St.' → one twenty-three West 42nd Street. '1300 E St NW' → thirteen hundred E Street Northwest: a single letter right before the type is the street's name. '300 E 23rd St' → three hundred East 23rd Street. '123-125 Main St.' → one twenty-three to one twenty-five Main Street. The type's period is dropped mid-sentence and kept as the full stop at the end of the text or before a sentence starter.
rules.risks: Skip when a quantity word or determiner comes before the number: over, under, about, around, nearly, almost, roughly, approximately, some, than, only, just, all, the, its, their, our, these, those. Skip a 4-digit number from 1000 to 2099 after a time word (in, since, by, until, before, after, during, of): 'In 2005 Ocean Drive was repaved' is frozen, while '…moved to 2005 Main St.' is an address (speech case). A number with a thousands separator or decimal point, or after $, # or No., is never a house number. New frozen near-misses: 'The 150 Federal Court judges', 'The 120 Times Square billboards', 'How 750 Oak Street Families Lost Power'. Only numbers of 3 or more digits change reading, so a misfire on 1–2 digits is harmless. A miss we accept: 'the 405 Freeway' has no name between the number and the type, so it stays 'four hundred five'.

rules.name: D. Street-type abbreviation after a street name
rules.trigger: Case-sensitive: (\p{Lu}[\p{L}'’-]*|\d{1,3}(?:st|nd|rd|th))\s+(Dr|Rd|Ln|Ct|Pl|Pkwy|Hwy|Cres|Terr|Ter|Sq|Cir|Trl|Ave)(\.)?(?![\p{L}\d]). The word before is captured and re-emitted. It must contain a lower-case letter (so not an acronym: 'ER Dr.', 'VA Dr.'), and must not be a sentence starter or a title. What follows must not be a capitalised name. Allowed after: end of text or line; [,;:)\]!?]; a lower-case word; a unit word (Suite, Ste, Apt, Unit, Fl, Floor, Rm, Room, Bldg, Building, #); a direction; a street-type or landmark word (Park, Square, Station); or a sentence starter after the period. A digit after the type is allowed only for Hwy, which then needs no name ('Take Hwy 401'). Dr only, extra condition: it also needs (a) a house number (rule C), (b) a place preposition right before the name with no article between (on, onto, off, along, down, up, at, to, from, near, past, via, across, into, toward, opposite, behind), or (c) a unit word, direction, ', City' or ZIP after it. Bare 'Ave' without a period gets the same test, which keeps 'Schubert's Ave Maria'.
rules.reads_as: Dr → Drive, Rd → Road, Ln → Lane, Ct → Court, Pl → Place, Pkwy → Parkway, Hwy → Highway, Cres → Crescent, Terr/Ter → Terrace, Sq → Square, Cir → Circle, Trl → Trail, Ave → Avenue. The period is handled as in rule C. 'Take Hwy 401 east' → Take Highway four oh one east.
rules.risks: Dr. before a capitalised name stays Doctor: 'Ask Dr. Patel', 'Head of Surgery Dr. Lee', 'Dr. Pepper' and 'Dr. Seuss' are frozen. The place-word condition on Dr is new. Without it, 'The ER Dr. said it was a sprain' read 'ER Drive' and 'Our Family Dr. retired' read 'Family Drive' (both now frozen). The cost is a miss: 'Mulholland Dr. is a David Lynch film' stays Doctor, so that case became 'We drove along Mulholland Dr. at dusk'. The digit condition keeps 'NFL Draft Rd. 1' (round) and 'Bar Ln 12' out. They aren't frozen because 'Rd.' reads 'ard' today. Pre-existing and outside this rule: the lexicon already reads 'Ct.' as 'court' everywhere, so 'Paper Towels, 12 Ct.' reads 'twelve court'. 'Heated Sq. ft.' would become 'Square ft.'; the units area should own 'Sq. ft.'. Today's readings: Rd. 'ard', Hwy 'hwI', Pkwy 'pikwI', Sq. 'S Q', Cres. 'krz', Terr. 'ter', Pl. 'P L', Dr. 'Doctor'.

rules.name: E. Direction after a street type
rules.trigger: A street type matched by rule C or D, or a full street-type word right after a capitalised name, followed by \s+(NE|NW|SE|SW)\.? and a boundary. A single N, S, E or W is allowed only inside a rule C match ('88 King St. W', '45 King St W').
rules.reads_as: Northeast, Northwest, Southeast, Southwest; North, South, East, West. '1600 Pennsylvania Ave. NW.' → … Avenue Northwest., with the final period kept as the full stop.
rules.risks: SE is a tech-lexicon term, so this belongs in the pre-pass. A lone letter outside an address stays as written: 'Sit in Row N, Seat 4' and 'Exit 9 W to the bridge' (new) are frozen, and 'Row' and 'Exit' are not street types. Position decides between a state and a direction: 'Omaha, NE' after 'City, ' is Nebraska (rule I), and NE after a street type is Northeast.

rules.name: F. St / Ste: Saint, Street or Suite
rules.where: TextNormalizer.readStreets (St. with a period) and TextNormalizer.addresses
rules.trigger: (1) 'St.' with a period, in readStreets: keep today's logic, and add one thing. After a capitalised word that isn't in Tokenizer.placePrefixes, St. before a landmark or time word is Street. The words: Station, Stn, Journal, Bridge, Market, Mall, Pier, Tunnel, Garage, Line, Subway, Bus, Exit, Gate, Festival, Fair, Parade, the days and the months. (2) 'St' with no period, before a capitalised word that isn't a sentence starter, is Saint when: the word before isn't capitalised; or it is a place prefix; or St starts the text ('We visited St Paul's', 'Mount St Helens'). After another capitalised word it is also Saint ('Yves St Laurent'), unless a landmark or time word follows ('Liverpool St Station' and 'The Wall St Journal' stay Street). It is never Saint when Tokenizer.isStreet holds. (3) 'Ste.' or 'Ste' before a capitalised name is Saint ('Sault Ste. Marie', 'Ste. Genevieve'). (4) 'Ste.' or 'Ste' before a number is Suite (rule G).
rules.risks: Today 'The Wall St. Journal', 'Liverpool St. Station is closed' and 'Bourbon St. Saturday night' all read Saint. Only 'at Liverpool St. Station' reads right, thanks to readStreets' street prepositions. 'Mount St. Helens', 'St. Louis' and 'Kings Cross St. Pancras' stay Saint: only the word right after St. counts, not one further on. Keep the landmark list short, and leave off saints whose names are also common nouns ('St. Cloud', 'St. Mark's', 'St. Bees'). 'St' without a period reads Street everywhere today, and 'Ste.' reads 'stee'.

rules.name: G. Unit designators, boxes and 'care of'
rules.trigger: (Ste|Suite|Apt|Apartment|Unit|Fl|Floor|Rm|Room|Bldg|Building)\.?\s*#?\s*(\d{1,4}[A-Z]?|[A-Z]\d{0,3})(?![\p{L}\d]), capitalised (or all capitals in a USPS address) and case-sensitive. Never right after 'City, '. Also: an ordinal followed by \s+Fl\.?; 'Bldg' or 'Bldg.' as a whole word; (P\.?\s?O\.?|Post Office)\s+Box\s+(\d+); and (?<![\p{L}\d/])[cC]/[oO](?![\p{L}\d/]) followed by \s+\p{Lu}.
rules.reads_as: Suite, Apartment, Unit, Floor, Room or Building, followed by the number from rule B. 'Rm. 214' → Room two fourteen; 'Room 101' → Room one oh one; 'Ste 1010' → Suite ten ten; 'Unit 302' → Unit three oh two; 'Apt 4C' → Apartment four C; '3rd Fl.' → third Floor; 'c/o Jane Smith' → care of Jane Smith.
rules.risks: At most 4 digits, and not after 'City, ': in 'Miami, Fl 33101' the Fl is Florida (rule I), not Floor. 'Room' and 'Box' are tech-lexicon terms, so the pass must see through their marks. A number must follow, so 'Apt to forget' and 'an apt name' stay as they are (frozen). Never touched: lower-case 'apt', 'fl.' and 'rm' (the Unix command), and 'RM 500' (ringgit). 'c/o' before a lower-case word stays letters ('Patient c/o chest pain' is frozen); 'c/o the front desk' is therefore a miss we accept.

rules.name: H. Route numbers
rules.trigger: (US|U\.S\.|Hwy\.?|Highway|Route|Rte\.?|SR|State Route|Interstate)\s+(\d{3})(?![\d.,%]). After the number must come: the end; punctuation; a direction word or letter; 'exit', 'freeway', 'highway' or 'bridge'; or a lower-case word that isn't a number word or unit (million, billion, thousand, percent, miles, km).
rules.reads_as: The 3-digit number from rule B: 'US 101 north' → U S one oh one north; 'Hwy 401' → Highway four oh one. Rte. reads Route (today it is spelled out letter by letter).
rules.risks: 'Route 66' keeps its cardinal (frozen). 'US 123 million' is ruled out by the follower check. 'I-405' already reads in pairs. 'The 405' with no keyword stays 'four hundred five', a miss we accept.

rules.name: I. US state codes after 'City, '
rules.trigger: A place, then ',[ \t]+', then an uppercase code, then a boundary. The place is the whole run of 1–4 capitalised words before the comma, after any leading sentence starters. St./Ft./Mt./Pt. prefixes, hyphens, apostrophes and de/del/la/du are allowed. Codes: the 50 states plus DC, PR, GU, VI, AS and MP. The code fires when either (a) a 5-digit ZIP follows with no digit right after it (the comma is then optional: 'AUSTIN TX 78701'), or (b) the pair (whole place run, code) is in a bundled US place list. The draft's path (c) is dropped: it accepted any place before a code that isn't an English word. Word-like codes (AL AR CA CO DE GA HI ID IL IN IA LA MA MD ME MI MO MS MT NE OH OK OR PA UT VA WA WI) need more under (b). They also need a place word before the run (in, to, from, near, at, of, outside, around, via, through, than, and, toward, into, across, an opening parenthesis, or 'based in'), or a verb right after the code (is, was, has, had, will, …), or a '-based' suffix, or a closing ')'. Territories fire only under (a), or under (b) with a place word. A title-case code ('Fl', 'Tx') counts only before a ZIP.
rules.reads_as: The full state name, keeping any suffix ('Oregon-based'). A final period stays as the full stop. DC stays 'D C'. PR → Puerto Rico, GU → Guam, VI → U S Virgin Islands, AS → American Samoa, MP → Northern Mariana Islands.
rules.risks: Path (c) was unsafe because other countries use the same two letters. Frozen examples: 'Chennai, TN' (Tamil Nadu), 'Florianópolis, SC' (Santa Catarina), 'Curitiba, PR' (Paraná), 'Bhopal, MP' (Madhya Pradesh). MN is also Manipur. Matching the whole run keeps 'Please welcome Amy Jackson, MS.' as letters (frozen), even though 'Jackson, MS' is a listed pair. OK is never Oklahoma before '?' or '!', or when 'OK,' is followed by a pronoun or 'let's'. 'Say hi to Norman, OK?', 'Enid, OK, let's go' and 'Fine, Norman, OK, you win' are frozen, while 'Have you been to Portland, OR?' still reads Oregon. A capitalised word right after the code blocks it ('Was it Portland, OR Seattle?' is frozen). The draft's guards still apply: interjections, personal titles, a credential after the code, and a ZIP required in a shouted sentence. Coverage now depends on the list. Use the full Census Gazetteer places file (about 32,000 incorporated places and CDPs, a few hundred KB) rather than 5,000 pairs. An unlisted town with no ZIP stays as letters ('Marfa, TX' → 'T X'), a miss we accept.

rules.name: J. AP-style state abbreviations after 'City, '
rules.trigger: A place, then ',\s+', then an AP abbreviation (Ala.|Ariz.|Ark.|Calif.|Colo.|Conn.|Del.|Fla.|Ga.|Ill.|Ind.|Kan.|Kans.|Ky.|La.|Md.|Mass.|Mich.|Minn.|Miss.|Mo.|Mont.|Neb.|Nebr.|Nev.|N.H.|N.J.|N.M.|N.Y.|N.C.|N.D.|Okla.|Ore.|Pa.|R.I.|S.C.|S.D.|Tenn.|Vt.|Va.|Wash.|W.Va.|Wis.|Wyo.). After it: a comma, the end, a ZIP, '(AP)', or a space and a lower-case word. The rule I place guards apply. Abbreviations that are also words or names (Miss., Pa., Mo., Ill., Ind., Mass., Wash., Del., La., Ga., Va., Conn., Mich., Ala., Md.) also need a listed (place, state) pair or a ZIP. Greetings and sign-offs never count as a place: Morning, Evening, Night, Goodnight, Love, Cheers, Regards, Best, Thanks, Yours.
rules.reads_as: The full state name: 'Salem, Ore., said' → Salem, Oregon, said; 'Albany, N.Y., is' → Albany, New York, is; 'Fresno, Calif.' at the end → California, with the full stop kept.
rules.risks: As first written, 'Morning, Miss.' read 'Mississippi', 'Goodnight, Pa.' read 'Pennsylvania' and 'Love, Mo.' read 'Missouri'. All three are frozen. Md. is a tech-lexicon term (read M D).

rules.name: K. ZIP codes
rules.trigger: (?<!\d)(\d{5})(?:-(\d{4}))?(?!\d), right after a state matched by rule I or J, or after ', <full state name> '. Also after 'ZIP', 'ZIP code', 'Zip code' or 'zip code', optionally followed by ':', 'is' or ','. A bare 'zip' or 'Zip' is not a trigger.
rules.reads_as: One digit at a time as words, with 0 read 'oh': '90210' → nine oh two one oh, '02110' → oh two one one oh. Emit words, not spaced digits, because '9 0 2 1 0' reads 'zero'. ZIP+4 is an open question.
rules.risks: 'Can you zip 25000 files at once?' is frozen. A 6-digit Indian PIN after a code ('Chennai, TN 600001') must not match on its first five digits. A bare 5-digit number stays a cardinal ('The stadium holds 70112 fans' is frozen). Today 90210 reads 'ninety thousand two hundred ten'.

rules.name: L. Canadian provinces and postal codes
rules.trigger: Provinces: a place, ',\s+', then (ON|QC|AB|MB|SK|NS|NB|PE|NL|YT|NU|NT|BC). It fires only when a postal code follows or the place is in a list of about 300 Canadian municipalities, and only before the same followers as rule I. A capitalised word right after the code blocks it. Postal codes, uppercase: (?<![\p{L}\d])([ABCEGHJ-NPRSTVXY])(\d)([ABCEGHJ-NPRSTV-Z])\s?(\d)([ABCEGHJ-NPRSTV-Z])(\d)(?![\p{L}\d]), only after a province code or name, 'Canada' or 'postal code'.
rules.reads_as: ON → Ontario, QC → Quebec, AB → Alberta, MB → Manitoba, SK → Saskatchewan, NS → Nova Scotia, NB → New Brunswick, PE → Prince Edward Island, NL → open question, YT → Yukon, NU → Nunavut, NT → Northwest Territories. BC stays 'B C'. A postal code is read one character at a time with a pause between the halves: 'T2P 1J9' → T two P, one J nine. Emit A so it reads as the letter.
rules.risks: 'Monterrey, NL' (Nuevo León) is frozen: Monterrey isn't a listed Canadian municipality. Today 'T2P' reads 'T to P' and 'AB' reads as a word. MB and NS are unit entries that apply only after a number, so there's no clash. 'H1N1' doesn't have the six-character shape.

rules.name: M. UK postcodes
rules.trigger: (?<![\p{L}\d])([A-PR-UWYZ][A-HK-Y]?\d[A-Z\d]?)[ ](\d[ABD-HJLNP-UW-Z]{2})(?![\p{L}\d]), uppercase, both halves with the space between; also 'GIR 0AA'. The inward letters must not be a storage unit (GB, TB, PB, EB). A place cue must come before the outward half: a capitalised place word, 'postcode' or 'Postcode:', a comma, or the start of a line.
rules.reads_as: Outward code: the letters as letter names and the digits as a number (SW19 → S W nineteen, B33 → B thirty-three, OX1 → O X one, EH1 → E H one). Then a pause. Inward code: the digit, then two letter names (5AE → five A E, 1AA → one A A). Z is 'zed' in the British voice.
rules.risks: 'The MacBook Air M2 8GB is enough' and 'Buy the PS5 1TB bundle' have the full postcode shape; both are frozen ('Galaxy S23 8GB' is the same). The inward letters exclude M, so '1PM' and '2AM' never match. Today: OX1 reads 'ox one', EH1 'eh one', 5AE 'five I', 1AE 'one I'. SW1A 1AA, SW1A 2AA and B33 8TH already read right.

rules.name: N. Australian states and postcodes; WA
rules.trigger: A place, ',?\s+', then (NSW|VIC|QLD|TAS|ACT|NT|SA|WA), optionally followed by \s+(\d{4}), then a boundary. With no postcode, it needs 'Place, ' at the end of a sentence or before punctuation, and the place can't be a greeting or sign-off word. Mixed-case 'Vic', 'Tas' and 'Qld' (with or without a period) fire only before a 4-digit postcode. For WA after a city: Western Australia (kept as letters) if a 4-digit postcode follows or the city is Australian; Washington if a 5-digit ZIP follows or the place is in the US list; otherwise it stays letters.
rules.reads_as: NSW → New South Wales, VIC → Victoria, QLD → Queensland, TAS → Tasmania. ACT, NT, SA and WA stay letters. A round-thousand postcode is read as a number (2000 → two thousand); any other postcode one digit at a time with 'oh' (3065 → three oh six five).
rules.risks: 'Cheers, Vic.' is frozen: as first written it read 'Victoria'. 'NSW Health' has no place before it (frozen). The ACT 2600 case was removed (open question), and 'Parliament House is in Canberra, ACT.' is frozen instead. NT clashes with Canada's Northwest Territories; what follows decides (4 digits means Australia).

rules.name: O. A single letter as a street name
rules.trigger: (Avenue|Ave\.?)\s+([A-Z])(?![\p{L}\d]), and ([A-Z])\s+(Street|St\.?)(?![\p{L}]) inside a rule C match or after a capitalised word or number.
rules.reads_as: The letter's name: 'Ave. A' → Avenue A (ˈA); '1300 E St' → E Street.
rules.risks: Today 'Ave. A' reads 'Avenue uh'. 'Avenue X', 'Avenue L' and 'Avenue V' (Brooklyn) read as letters today and must not become Roman numerals ('Get off at Avenue X.' is frozen); after Avenue, the letter outranks readRomanNumerals. 'Plan A' has no street word, so it is untouched.

open_questions: Five-digit house numbers ('10548 Ventura Blvd.'): read one digit at a time ('one oh five four eight') or in groups ('ten five forty-eight')? Recommend one digit at a time, with round thousands kept whole. The ESL Cafe street-number guide reads 5+ digits this way.

ZIP+4 ('Chicago, IL 60601-1234'): 'six oh six oh one, one two three four' (pause) or 'six oh six oh one dash one two three four'? Both are common, so the case was removed until this is decided. Recommend the pause for reading aloud.
Zero in ZIP codes, postcodes and house or room numbers: 'oh' or 'zero'? Recommend 'oh', the habit in both US and UK speech.

Rule I's draft path (c) is dropped because it read 'Chennai, TN' as Tennessee and 'Florianópolis, SC' as South Carolina. Should the place list grow to the full Census Gazetteer (about 32,000 places and CDPs, a few hundred KB) to win back coverage? Otherwise unlisted towns with no ZIP stay as letters ('Marfa, TX'). Recommend the full list.

Dr. with no house number and no place word ('Mulholland Dr. is a David Lynch film'): accept 'Doctor' (a miss), or read Drive after any capitalised word that isn't an acronym (which also turns 'Our Family Dr. retired' into Drive)? Recommend accepting the miss.

British voice and 3-digit numbers: should 221B and room 214 be read digit by digit ('two two one B', 'room two one four') when the voice is British? Both cases are US-only until this is decided. 'Room 101' is 'one oh one' in both.
Canada's 'NL': 'Newfoundland' or 'Newfoundland and Labrador'? The St. John's case was removed until this is decided. Recommend 'Newfoundland'.

Australian postcodes: digit by digit except round thousands ('three oh six five', 'two thousand')? And is Canberra's 2600 'two six oh oh' or 'twenty-six hundred'? I found no source on Australian speech; a check with an Australian listener would help.
'PE' (Prince Edward Island): read 'Prince Edward Island' or 'P E I'? Recommend 'Prince Edward Island'.
review_notes: The worktree moved during the review. The fix3/reading merge (b06b926) rebuilt the binary at 14:59 and added TextNormalizer.readStreets. Everything below was re-run on that binary. Today 7 of 104 US cases and 7 of 101 British cases pass. Five more (P.O. Box, the BC postcode, SW1A 2AA, B33 8TH and one other already-right case) pass only once spaces are ignored. Every frozen case reads correctly today in both voices.

Rule-text checks on every 'says' (scripted): no digits, symbols, abbreviations, all-capital tokens or Roman numerals. Letters are written as spaced capitals ('D C', 'P O', 'U S', 'S W'), and the letter A is written 'ay' because a lone 'A' reads as the article. Every 'says' sentence went through --phonemize in both voices with no unknown words. One misreading is shared by text and says: 'Sault' reads 'salt', a names issue noted on that case.

Expectations fixed or removed. The Chicago ZIP+4 case became a plain ZIP: '-1234' is read two ways. The St. John's 'NL' case was removed (name question). The Canberra 'ACT 2600' case became a frozen 'Canberra, ACT.' because the postcode reading is unsettled. 221B and Rm. 214 are now US-only, since British speakers often say 'two two one B' and 'two one four'. The added comma in 'Austin, Texas' was removed so the says matches the text. The '7 Elm St.' note was corrected: it reads right since readStreets.

'Mulholland Dr. is a David Lynch film' became 'We drove along Mulholland Dr. at dusk'. Rule D now needs a place word or a house number before Dr, because without one 'The ER Dr. said…' and 'Our Family Dr. retired…' read Drive.

Frozen cases removed. 'Thanks, MA!' reads 'M A' today, which is wrong for 'Ma'; freezing it would lock in a misreading. 'Come on, AL!' reads 'Al' in US and 'A L' in British, so it would block a letters fix. Also trimmed as low-value duplicates: Thanks Dr. Lee, Dr. No, Fine OK, He said OK, Press OK, Not you ME, Choose IN or OUT, GA now, MD will see you, from the US, Main Street was busy, A4 sheet, Chapter 123, Suite 200, Apartment 4B, Number 4 Privet Drive.

30 new frozen near-misses, each one something a draft rule would have rewritten. Dr: 'ER Dr.', 'Family Dr.', 'your Dr.'. St: 'Liverpool St Station', 'Wall St Journal'. Letters: 'Avenue X' (Roman numeral). OK and OR: Enid, Norman, 'Portland, OR Seattle'. Country codes. 'Amy Jackson, MS'. Foreign regions that share US codes: Chennai TN, Florianópolis SC, Curitiba PR, Bhopal MP, Monterrey NL. 'NSW Health'. AP-style words and names: Miss., Pa., Mo., Vic. Non-addresses: 'Federal Court judges', 'Times Square billboards', a title-case headline, '2005' as a year, 'zip 25000 files', 'Route 66', 'Exit 9 W', 'OH, I get it'. UK postcode look-alikes: 'M2 8GB' and 'PS5 1TB'.

Rules tightened in response: A, C, D, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N and O; details are in each rule. The biggest changes: rule I drops path (c) and matches the whole place run; rule C needs an address cue before a spelled-out street type and skips years; rule D needs a place word before Dr; rule M won't take storage units; rule K drops bare 'zip' as a cue.

New positive cases from real text. Shipping and receipts: USPS-capitals 'OAK DR' (DR is a marked term), an all-capitals receipt with '1ST ST', Evergreen Terrace, Ste 1010, Unit 302. Company addresses: Apple Park and Microsoft, whose cities Cupertino and Redmond are marked terms; Wacker Dr Suite 1500; Wilshire 4400. Chat: 'Meet at 1250 Oak Ave?'. 'Born in 2005… 2005 Main St.' (a year and a house number in one sentence). E as a street name vs East. Hwy 401. Miami 'Fl 33101' (must not be Floor). Kansas City, St. Paul, Bloomington, Fresno 'Calif.', 'Portland, OR?'. St. bugs that exist today: 'Wall St. Journal', 'Liverpool St. Station' and 'Bourbon St. Saturday' read Saint; 'Mount St Helens' and 'Yves St Laurent' read Street. Also SW1A 2AA, a UK flat address, Martin Pl in Sydney.

The set is larger than the target (104 speech cases, 72 frozen) after trimming duplicates. It keeps US, Canadian, Australian and UK coverage and one near-miss per new rule condition. The parent can drop the 'already right' cases if size matters.

Carried over from the author and still needed: the harness keeps word boundaries, so 'P O Box' (pˈi ˈO) never matches today's 'P.O.' (pˌiˈO). Also, the British voice reads 'forty-two' differently from 'forty two'. Before phonemizing 'says', replace a hyphen between letters with a space, and compare with all whitespace removed. The scripted checks here did exactly that.

Frozen British cardinals ('The 150 Federal Court judges' reads 'one hundred fifty', with no 'and') lock in today's British numbers. If a numbers change adds the British 'and', re-freeze them; that is not an address regression.

Research: house-number reading patterns (grouped vs digit by digit; 5+ digits with 'oh') come from the ESL Cafe guide, https://eslcafe.com/resources/grammar-lessons/saying-numbers/saying-street-numbers. I found no source on how Australians speak postcodes or how British speakers say 3-digit house numbers; both are open questions.
